strengths: Addresses a practically important and timely problem: Bayesian optimization with many observations (BOMO) driven by cheap simulations and parallel evaluation
Novel K-nearest-neighbor surrogate (ENN) that elegantly avoids O(N²) kernel matrix construction while providing principled uncertainty estimates (epistemic and aleatoric), achieving O(N ln K) scaling
Strong empirical results: 1-2 orders of magnitude speedup in proposal time (12-150×) while maintaining comparable solution quality across diverse problems with up to 50,000 observations
Rigorous theoretical contribution: Shows TuRBO-ENN satisfies PseudoBO conditions (LC, SNEB, IP) with clean proofs in Appendix A, guaranteeing convergence
Thoughtful practical variants: Noise-free variant with non-dominated sorting avoids fitting overhead; natural vs. frozen noise experiments show method works in realistic settings
Comprehensive experimental scope: Five diverse problems (2D physics simulations, 34D control, 180D hyperparameter optimization), both noise settings, clear scaling visualization
Clear presentation: Paper is well-written with effective figures; O(N) vs O(N²) scaling gap in Figure 1 is compelling; code availability aids reproducibility
weaknesses: Method design lacks principled justification: (1) Independence assumption for observations made 'for tractability' contradicts actual data dependencies—no analysis of when this breaks down; (2) Epistemic variance model σ_e²(x|x_m) = c_e·d²(x,x_m) is ad-hoc—no justification for squared distance, no ablation studies; (3) Conditional mean property unusual in precision-weighted averaging context

Critical hyperparameter K fixed at 10 without sensitivity analysis: No ablation on K ∈ {5,10,20,50,100}; unclear how K should scale with D or N; authors acknowledge K selection as 'future work' but this should be addressed empirically given its direct impact on speed and uncertainty

Missing key experimental comparisons: No empirical evaluation of neural networks (Snoek et al. 2015) or random forests (Hutter et al. 2011) despite dismissing them as 'complex'; Vecchia GP only in Figure 1 not main experiments; no comparison to modern sparse GP methods; CMA-ES performance under-discussed

Insufficient experimental analysis: (1) No hyperparameter sensitivity for c_e, s_0, subsample size P; (2) No statistical significance testing despite showing error bars; (3) Timing breakdown missing—cannot separate fitting from acquisition time to attribute speedups; (4) Subsampled LOOCV justification is statistical but empirical comparison to full LOOCV absent

Theoretical gaps: PseudoBO provides consistency but authors explicitly provide no regret bounds; no convergence rate analysis or empirical comparison of rates between TuRBO and TuRBO-ENN; no analysis of when ENN's limited extrapolation (bounded by max K-NN distance) becomes problematic

Acquisition method swap under-explored: Replacing Thompson sampling (known to have near-optimal regret guarantees) with UCB or NDS is justified for speed but motivates limited ablation—unclear how much solution quality differences stem from surrogate vs. acquisition change

Limited experimental scope: All benchmarks are simulations or HPO; no real-world BO applications (A/B testing, materials science) mentioned in introduction but not tested; limited to D ≤ 180 despite curse-of-dimensionality issues with Euclidean distance acknowledged but not addressed

Uncertainty calibration unvalidated: No quantitative analysis of calibration (e.g., coverage plots, calibration curves); Figure 2 shows ENN doesn't interpolate (good) but systematic comparison to GP uncertainty quality missing

High-dimensional issues not addressed: Paper acknowledges 'As D increases, Euclidean distance discriminates less' but provides no solution (no dimension weighting, no ARD); Frozen vs. natural noise speedups conflated—larger speedups for frozen noise largely due to skipped fitting, not method advantage

Reproducibility gaps: Some Algorithm 1 details defer to original TuRBO papers (trust region mechanics, RAASP); full reproducibility from paper alone challenging; O(N ln K) complexity is understated—nearest-neighbor search compounding not fully characterized for massive N

strengths: Well-motivated BOMO problem with practical relevance for fast simulations and parallel evaluation
Impressive practical speedups (10-150× reduction in proposal time) with competitive solution quality on tested problems
Formal theoretical grounding via Pseudo-Bayesian Optimization framework with convergence guarantees
Clear presentation with good motivation and informative figures (especially scaling demonstration)
Practical dual-variant design (fitting-free for noise-free problems via NDS)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: K-NN surrogates in BO are established (prior work by Gramacy & Apley, Jimenez & Katzfuss, Wu et al.); contribution is incremental engineering rather than methodological innovation
Fundamental unresolved limitation: curse of dimensionality acknowledged but not addressed, severely limiting applicability to high-dimensional problems (D>50)
Overly restrictive ENN assumptions: independence assumption unrealistic, distance-based variance σ²_e=c_e·d²(x,x_m) is simplistic, raw-value conditional means lack smoothing—impacts unknown
Critical hyperparameter P (LOOCV subsampling size) is never specified in paper; K fixed at 10 without justification or sensitivity analysis
Narrow experimental validation: only 5 problems (mostly RL simulations), problem selection biased toward favorable characteristics, no statistical significance testing, missing ablation studies
Theory-practice gap: PseudoBO provides only asymptotic convergence guarantee without rates or regret bounds; β=1 in UCB unjustified
Frozen noise experiments are unrealistic and inflate apparent benefits; fitting-free variant only applies in this unrepresentative setting
No empirical validation that independence and distance-variance assumptions do not significantly harm performance
Incomplete comparisons: neural network/random forest surrogates excluded, limited comparison to recent scalable BO methods

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated practical problem (BOMO) with clear distinction from traditional BO and HDBO
Achieves impressive empirical speedups of 10-150× in proposal time while maintaining competitive solution quality across 5 diverse benchmarks
Demonstrates genuine scalability with experiments up to 50,000 observations
Provides theoretical grounding: rigorously proves TuRBO-ENN satisfies Pseudo-Bayesian Optimization conditions (LC, SNEB, IP) in Appendix A, guaranteeing convergence
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including both natural and frozen noise, 30 runs with error bars, and clear scaling analysis showing O(N) behavior
Well-engineered with two acquisition variants (fitting-free NDS for noise-free, UCB for noisy) and practical design choices
Clear presentation and reproducible algorithm specification (Algorithm 1)
Code availability promised via pip-installable library
weaknesses: Critical design choices lack justification: K=10 is fixed throughout with no ablation study, β=1 in UCB is unexplained, and distance² for epistemic variance has no principled justification—statement 'we find that K=10 gives good performance' is insufficient
Independence assumption in ENN explicitly made 'for tractability' but never validated empirically—impact on performance is unknown
Missing direct experimental comparison to Vecchia GP methods mentioned in related work (Section 3), despite being closest related approach with similar K-nearest-neighbor philosophy
No ablation studies on K, P (subsampling size), or β; no sensitivity analysis on variance functional forms—leaves uncertainty about robustness
Uncertainty quantification not validated: no calibration analysis, no comparison of ENN vs GP uncertainties, uncertainty only used for acquisition decisions
Limited experimental scope: only 5 test problems (mostly D≤34, only one D=180 problem), all appear relatively smooth/structured, no adversarial cases or standard benchmarks (BBOB)
High-dimensional performance underexplored despite noting that 'Euclidean distance discriminates less between observations' as D increases (Section 6)

Hyperparameter fitting details incomplete: variance justification for fixed P assumes unbiased estimators (unproven for subsampled version), optimization algorithm unspecified, no guidance for choosing P in practice
Noise-free variant feels incomplete: defaults s₀=0, cₑ=1 are never ablated; justification that 'NDS never compares σ to μ directly' seems to leave performance on the table
Only convergence guarantee provided (via Chen & Lam 2025), no regret bounds or sample complexity analysis; limited independent theoretical contribution
Statistical analysis lacks rigor: no significance tests, ±2SE error bars without formal testing, natural-noise 'passive evaluation' metric is non-monotonic making comparison difficult
No breakdown of wall-clock time (fitting vs acquisition vs candidate generation) or per-iteration timing analysis to understand where speedups originate

strengths: Clear problem formulation and motivation: BOMO regime is practically important and well-distinguished from HDBO. Addresses real bottleneck where proposal time dominates in fast-evaluation settings.
Dramatic empirical speedups: Consistent 8-151× reductions in proposal time across five diverse simulators with up to 50,000 observations, while maintaining competitive solution quality.

Solid theoretical foundation: Comprehensive analysis proving ENN satisfies PBO conditions (local consistency, sequential no-empty-ball, improvement property) with bias-variance bounds and convergence guarantees.

Thorough experimental methodology: Proper handling of natural vs. frozen noise, extensive ablations on K and P, 30 runs per configuration with appropriate baselines, isolation of fitting vs. acquisition costs.

Thoughtful algorithmic contributions: Fitting-free variant for noise-free problems via non-dominated sorting, justified subsampled LOOCV for hyperparameter fitting, separation of epistemic/aleatoric uncertainties.
Strong reproducibility: Open-source package promised, detailed algorithm specification, comprehensive hyperparameter documentation, and accessible baseline implementations.
Honest limitations discussion: Acknowledges fixed K, missing Thompson sampling, high-dimensional challenges, constraint handling—demonstrates mature treatment of limitations.
weaknesses: Heuristic uncertainty quantification lacking probabilistic grounding: Epistemic variance purely based on distance (σ²_e = c_e·d²) rather than derived from principled probabilistic model. Unlike GPs, no formal interpretation of posterior or uncertainty calibration guarantees.

Strong independence assumption for tractability: Treating all observations as independent estimates may not hold in practice; impact on method behavior not thoroughly investigated. This simplification seems to sacrifice modeling power without clear justification.

Limited algorithmic novelty: While ENN formulation is new, K-NN and Vecchia approximation approaches address similar problems (noted in related work). Core contribution is demonstrating simpler methods suffice for speed—useful but incremental rather than methodologically novel.

Arbitrary design choices without principled justification: Fixed K=10 across all problems despite showing problem-dependent sensitivity in ablations; replacement of Thompson sampling with UCB for speed rather than theoretical reasons; subsampling justification relies on variance argument without practical guidance.

Narrow applicability limited to BOMO regime: Method specifically optimized for scenarios with many observations and moderate dimensions. High-dimensional scaling remains poor (acknowledged). In practice, evaluation cost often dominates proposal time, limiting real-world impact.

No improvement in solution quality: TuRBO-ENN matches but does not exceed TuRBO performance. Speed gains are valuable but primary contribution is computational efficiency rather than better optimization.

Theory-practice gap: Theorems assume exact observations and Lipschitz continuity; practical conditions for convergence guarantees not discussed. Connection between abstract theoretical results (Theorems 1-3) and Algorithm 1 implementation remains implicit.

Limited analysis of failure modes and problem-dependent behavior: Only highly-multimodal Ackley shows significant K sensitivity; insufficient exploration of when distance-based uncertainty estimation fails or succeeds relative to alternatives.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem: scaling BO to settings with many cheap observations shows significant real-world importance
Impressive and consistent empirical speedups: 8.5× to 151× reduction in proposal time across multiple diverse simulators with up to 50,000 observations, without sacrificing solution quality
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple realistic simulators, both natural and frozen noise settings, extensive ablations, good comparison against relevant baselines

Solid theoretical analysis: Rigorous proofs of local consistency, sequential no-empty-ball properties, weighted-kNN bias-variance bounds, and verification of Pseudo-Bayesian Optimization conditions providing convergence guarantees
Practical clever design: The fitting-free variant for noise-free problems (non-dominated sorting over µ and σ) effectively leverages problem structure and achieves additional speedups
Clear presentation: Well-structured paper with effective visualizations, particularly Figure 1 demonstrating scaling behavior across methods
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: ENN is essentially weighted K-NN with distance-based uncertainty—applying existing ideas rather than developing fundamentally new methodology. K-NN surrogates for BO are not novel (Vecchia methods, nearest-neighbor GP approaches)

Unjustified core design choice: The epistemic variance formula σ²_e = c_e d²(x, x_m) lacks rigorous justification beyond intuition. Why squared distance? Why this functional form? This critical modeling choice that defines the uncertainty estimates needs principled grounding, not just intuition

Confounded experimental comparisons: TuRBO uses Thompson sampling while TuRBO-ENN uses UCB/non-dominated sorting. Critically, Appendix A.3 shows turbo-one-ucb (TuRBO with UCB) performs similarly to original TuRBO, suggesting speedups may come from acquisition method change rather than surrogate change, confounding the key comparison

Ad-hoc hyperparameter selection: K fixed to 10 without principled justification (only post-hoc ablations), P held constant independent of N using informal variance arguments rather than principled selection criteria

Incomplete surrogate comparisons: No direct Bayesian optimization performance comparison to neural network (DNGO) or random forest (SMAC) surrogates—dismissed as complex without empirical BO comparison. Only pure fitting tasks shown, not what matters for optimization

Problem-specific speedup: Main speedup advantage for noise-free problems comes from skipping hyperparameter fitting entirely, limiting generality. For real noisy problems, fitting is still required, undermining the universality of claimed speedups

Incomplete solution quality evidence: Claims 'comparable-quality solutions' but evidence is mixed. Natural noise plots show high variance and non-monotonic behavior. turbo-zero (surrogate-free) performs surprisingly well on frozen noise, questioning whether surrogate quality matters
Limited theoretical guarantees: Explicitly acknowledges 'we provide no regret bounds'—only convergence, which is weaker than theoretical guarantees available for GP-based methods (Srinivas et al.)
Modeling assumptions lack justification: Independence assumption for tractability is significant but not validated. Impact of independence loss on uncertainty quantification is unanalyzed
Limited high-dimensional analysis: Acknowledges that Euclidean distance becomes uninformative in high dimensions but provides only superficial treatment. Most experiments use moderate D (≤180)
Experimental setup limitations: All benchmarks are cheap, fast simulations (not expensive evaluations) and use sequential runs—misaligned with the motivated use case of parallel expensive simulations

Incomplete scalability analysis: Finding K nearest neighbors is O(N ln K), not strictly O(N). Constant factors matter in practice but are not analyzed. Unclear how method scales for large candidate sets

strengths: Clear problem motivation distinguishing BOMO from HDBO, addressing increasingly practical regime of cheap simulations and parallel evaluation
Substantial practical speedups (1-2 orders of magnitude reduction in proposal time across diverse benchmarks, with improvements scaling with N)
Maintains competitive solution quality compared to TuRBO despite surrogate simplification
Strong theoretical grounding with Theorem 1 (ENN properties), Theorem 2 (bias-variance bounds), and Theorem 3 (fitted parameter transfer) providing PBO convergence guarantees

Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning 5 simulation tasks and HPO problem with 30 runs per setting, multiple noise models (natural/frozen), and diverse baselines including Optuna, SMAC, CMA-ES, DNGO, Vecchia GP
Clever design choices including subsampled LOO likelihood with variance-based justification for constant P, and noise-free variant via non-dominated sorting
Excellent reproducibility with open-source pip-installable package, detailed algorithm specification, and ablation studies on sensitive parameters K and P
Thorough ablation studies demonstrating robustness and pure fitting task evaluation showing ENN surrogate quality
weaknesses: Independence assumption treating observations as independent for tractability is simplification; impact on uncertainty calibration for nearby design points not fully analyzed
Subsampled LOO likelihood convergence properties inadequately characterized; does hyperparameter estimate quality degrade at very large N? Formal analysis limited
Fixed K=10 throughout all BO runs is rigid despite ablations showing sensitivity; paper lacks principled guidance for selecting K for particular problems
No regret bounds provided (acknowledged); PBO convergence guarantees are weaker theoretical guarantees compared to traditional BO regret analysis
Solution quality improvements on natural-noise problems appear marginal with substantially overlapping error bands across methods; 'comparable quality' claim not visually compelling
Incomplete timeout comparisons in Table 1: methods exceeding 5-hour budget marked '>5hr' without distinguishing non-completion from slow completion
Limited analysis of failure modes or problem characteristics favoring GPs over ENN; curse of dimensionality potential for high-D problems not thoroughly studied
Cannot perform Thompson sampling with ENN due to lack of joint sample support, limiting compatibility with TS-based acquisition methods
Moderate novelty: combines existing components (KNN surrogates + trust regions) in straightforward way; specific ENN formulation is novel but not groundbreaking
Narrow scope restricted to BOMO regime; for expensive-to-evaluate functions or small N, traditional BO remains preferred, limiting general applicability
